newsitem.title: USA: Ill. lawmaker says House may not pay for COPs.
newsitem.headline: Ill. lawmaker says House may not pay for COPs.

text.p: An Illinois lawmaker who is leading a lawsuit challenging the legality of a $19.2 million certificates of participation issue said Friday that Democrats in the Illinois House may not be willing to appropriate funds for debt service payments on the issue.
"The Illinois House will not be inclined to make lease payments," said State Rep. Jeff Schoenberg, D-Evanston, who hinted that he might be the new chairman of the House Appropriations Committee.
Those lease payments are expected to be included in a fiscal 1998 budget that Gov. Jim Edgar will propose in March.

Mike Colsch, Illinois' deputy budget director, declined to comment on the budget. He said, however, that the state would do "whatever we need to do to make the lease payments we're committed to make."
"We're not going to do anything that would jeapordize our credit rating," he said.
On Wednesday, Democrats took over control of the House from Republicans as a result of the Nov. 5 election.
Schoenberg said the House may hold "extensive hearings" in the coming weeks on the state's use of COPs.

Schoenberg was one of six Democrats from the House who filed the lawsuit on June 10 claiming the February sale of the COPs as part of a lease-purchase agreement entered into by the Illinois Department of Central Management Services exceeded that agency's constitutional and statutory authority. The lease-purchase agreement was for a Illinois Public Aid building currently under construction in downtown Chicago.

Meanwhile, MBIA Insurance Corp, which insured the $19.2 million of COPs, met last month with Schoenberg and then-prospective House Speaker Michael Madigan, D-Chicago, to discuss the litigation, according to Jack Guthman, a Chicago attorney representing MBIA.

Guthman said while MBIA is not a party to the lawsuit, the insurer wanted to alert lawmakers that the lawsuit could have broader ramifications beyond the $19.2 million COPs issue to Illinois' future debt issuance.

He added that MBIA offered a "reasonable approach" to the matter that he declined to explain. He also said the insurer wants to continue to have an active role in the state and plans to meet with representatives of the Edgar Administration and Republican legislative leadership.
The lawsuit continues to chug along in Cook County Circuit Court, where the developer of the building filed a motion Friday to change the judge hearing the case.
An attorney representing developer, National Build to Suit Clinton L.L.C., was not available to comment. The developer was added as a defendant in the lawsuit in September at the state's request.
Schoenberg said the motion, which the lawmakers are contesting, would only serve to slow down the lawsuit if granted.
"We've said all along and we said in court it's merely a legal tactic to shop for someone who might tell them what they want to hear," he said.
Brad Kapnick, an attorney at Sidley & Austin, who is representing Illinois central management services, said the state took no position on the motion to remove Judge Michael Getty from the case.
Getty scheduled a March 4 hearing on the motion.

Lawyers for the state had initially pressed Getty to expedite the lawsuit saying the litigation clouded the state's ability to use COPs to finance needed prison construction. That pressure appeared to ease in the fall, when Madigan said Democrats would support general obligation bonds for prisons.

However, Madigan's proposal for $201 million of GO bonding authority failed to move in the fall veto session of the General Assembly, as Republicans pushed for a $610 million bonding bill that went beyond prison funding. The Republicans' bill failed to muster a required three-fifths vote to pass.
Steve Brown, a spokesman for Madigan, said the speaker is mulling a new GO bonding bill for prisons and local schools.
